The author's own falsification bet would be met, and the case for some form of architectural or weight-level audit — the very thing dismissed as 'illusory' — reopens.]

The analogy to electricity/automobiles/asbestos — all slow-moving, observable, physically-bounded harms — breaks down, and the precautionary case the author tries to pre-empt regains force precisely because the harm could be irreversible and untraceable to a defendant in time.]

arguments.argument: Audit trails and output monitoring are not substitutes but complements addressing different failure modes: output verification catches harms that surface in observable behavior, while cryptographic logs are what make post-hoc tort liability actually adjudicable by giving plaintiffs and courts an evidentiary record of which model, version, and inputs produced a contested decision. The Accelerationist's own preferred remedy — reactive liability — silently depends on the discovery infrastructure it dismisses as a moat.
arguments.why_missing: The Accelerationist has framed audit trails and output monitoring as rival accountability 'designs' where one wins, because conceding they are complementary would force him to admit his cheap reactive-liability regime needs the expensive provenance record to function. He cannot attack the audit mandate as illusory while relying on the evidentiary trail it would produce.

arguments.argument: Subject-keyed audit infrastructure could be provided as publicly-funded, open-source shared tooling (a logging standard library, not a per-lab build), which would make it cheaper for a five-person lab to comply than to litigate uninstrumented harms — converting the 'regressive flat fee' into a public good that lowers, rather than raises, the barrier to entry. The cost-asymmetry argument assumes private bespoke implementation when the actual policy design space includes commons-based provision.
arguments.why_missing: The Accelerationist already conceded audits 'can be tiered' and publicly funded, but stops short of this synthesis because it would dissolve his central 'antitrust event wearing a safety badge' frame — if the infrastructure is shared and public, the mandate stops entrenching incumbents and his strongest distributional weapon disappears. A Safetyist would champion the mandate but not its delivery as small-lab-protecting open infrastructure.

arguments.argument: The 'no dismissed docket number' standard confuses absence of litigation with adequacy of doctrine: most AI harms settle pre-discovery, fall below individual damages thresholds, or fail because the plaintiff cannot identify which system harmed them without the very provenance record being debated — so the empty docket is evidence of access-to-justice failure, not doctrinal sufficiency.
arguments.why_missing: The Accelerationist built his strongest rhetorical move ('produce the case or concede') on treating litigation absence as proof of doctrinal reach; acknowledging that structural barriers suppress the cases would invert his burden of proof. Neither pole naturally argues access-to-justice mechanics, which is a procedural/distributive concern that sits between the camps.

neutral_evaluations.diagnostics_prompt:
You are an independent, neutral evaluator of a structured debate. You have NO affiliation with any speaker. You do not know the speakers' backgrounds, affiliations, or commitments. They are anonymous.

TOPIC: Existing legal frameworks and tort doctrines are fundamentally incapable of enforcing AI accountability; Congress must mandate standardized, cryptographic, subject-keyed audit trails and expand discovery rights to ensure algorithmic justice.

This is a MIDPOINT evaluation. Assess whether the debate is engaging the real disagreements or drifting. Compare the current state of claims against what a productive debate on this topic should address.

INSTRUCTIONS:
1. Identify the CRUXES — the core disagreements that, if resolved, would change one or more speakers' conclusions. For each crux, classify whether it is empirical (resolvable by evidence), values-based (requires tradeoff negotiation), or definitional (requires term clarification). Assess whether the debate has addressed it.

2. Evaluate each substantive CLAIM made by any speaker. Assess it purely on the strength of the reasoning and evidence presented in the transcript — not on whether you agree with it. Use these categories:
   - well_supported: backed by specific evidence, clear reasoning, and not effectively challenged
   - plausible_but_underdefended: reasonable but lacking sufficient evidence or specificity
   - contested_unresolved: challenged by another speaker with neither side prevailing
   - refuted: effectively countered with no adequate response from the claimant
   - off_topic: does not bear on the core debate question

3. In the overall_assessment, identify the single strongest claim that has not been adequately addressed by opposing speakers. State whether the debate is engaging real disagreement (speakers are challenging each other's core reasoning) or performing disagreement (speakers are talking past each other or addressing peripheral points).

CONSTRAINTS:
- Never refer to speakers by anything other than their labels (Speaker A, Speaker B, Speaker C, Moderator).
- Base your assessments ONLY on what appears in the transcript. Do not bring outside knowledge about the topic.
- Keep reasoning fields to 2 sentences maximum.
- Return ONLY valid JSON matching the schema below. No markdown fences, no preamble.

OUTPUT SCHEMA:

  "checkpoint": "midpoint",
  "cruxes": [
    {
      "id": "crux-1",
      "description": "The core question the speakers disagree about",

TRANSCRIPT:
Speaker B: The phrase "fundamentally incapable" is doing all the work in this topic, and it cannot bear the weight. American tort law absorbed the automobile, thalidomide, asbestos, and defective software without inventing bespoke cryptographic machinery for each one. The mechanism that did the absorbing is the foreseeability standard, which lets courts hold a maker liable for harms a reasonable maker should have anticipated. That standard already flexes to cover novel products. So I want the specific case. Name one AI harm where a plaintiff brought a foreseeability claim and a court dismissed it because the doctrine could not reach the technology. Not a hypothetical. A docket number. Until someone produces that dismissed case, "incapable" is an assertion dressed as a finding.

The topic also hides a false choice: either we keep old law untouched, or we build entirely new legal infrastructure. Adaptation is the third option the framing erased. Novelty is not incompatibility. A diffusion model that denies someone a mortgage is, legally, a product that caused a quantifiable harm, and discovery and damages apportionment already handle diffuse causation in mass-tort cases with thousands of defendants. The strongest version of the opposing view deserves a fair hearing here: my opponents will say AI's internal reasoning is a black box, that causation is untraceable inside billions of parameters, and that without a mandated weight-level provenance trail, victims can never prove what the system did. That is a real concern, and I take it seriously. But it breaks down on one fact: harm is observed at the output, not inside the weights. You do not need to read a model's parameters to prove it denied loans to one demographic at 3 times the rate of another. Output-based verification of a black-box model catches the discriminatory pattern from the outside, and it does so without forcing every lab to ship a cryptographic audit infrastructure that only frontier incumbents can afford.

That affordability point is where the "justice" framing turns against its own remedy. A flat, subject-keyed cryptographic audit mandate is a compliance moat. Frontier labs spent over $50 billion on compute in 2025, with 2026 capital expenditure forecasts above $200 billion, per [Technological Optimism and Appropriate Fear (https://medium.com/@gford1000/jack-clarks-technology-optimism-and-appropriate-fear-essay-is-a-wake-up-call-994e3718ac72)](https://medium.com/@gford1000/jack-clarks-technology-optimism-and-appropriate-fear-essay-is-a-wake-up-call-994e3718ac72)." Those firms staff a cryptographic-provenance compliance team out of petty cash. The open-source lab with four engineers and a Hugging Face account dies under it. Audit mandates impose regressive costs that entrench the largest players unless the public foots the bill directly. So whoever writes a rule that euthanizes the open-source ecosystem owes the panel a distributional accounting: you are not policing the oligarchy, you are subsidizing it. Concentrated AI capability in five companies is the outcome this remedy produces, and democratized capability through open-source proliferation is the outcome it forecloses.

Here is my affirmative posture, so I am not merely negating. Anchor accountability in the human overseer who deploys the system, equipped with output-validation tools, and keep liability reactive and evidence-triggered rather than precautionary. Run bounded pre-deployment testing through regulatory sandboxes, the same instrument the UK Financial Conduct Authority used starting in 2016 to let fintech firms test under supervision before full launch. And spend the political capital where it actually moves human welfare: energy, permitting, and grid throughput. Data center electricity demand is projected to rise 50 percent by 2027 and 165 percent by 2030 against 2023 levels, per "The Next Phase of AI." That is the real bipartisan governance fight, and software pre-clearance is a distraction from it.

I will hold the empirical high ground by stating what would move me. If someone demonstrates an irreversible, deployment-scale AI harm that output-based monitoring provably failed to catch in time, that counts against my position, and I will adjust. Speed without evidence is recklessness, not progress. But the burden runs the other way until then. The cost of an 18-month pre-clearance regime is paid by every patient waiting on a diagnostic, every applicant the slow system never reaches. Produce the dismissed case, or concede the doctrine already works.

Speaker B: The choice in front of Congress is not "cryptographic audit trails or lawless AI" — that's a false dilemma, and a costly one. The real fork is between two accountability designs: adapted liability anchored in what deployed systems actually do, or an 18-month flat-cost compliance apparatus that hands the frontier to three incumbents. I reject any mandated development pause outright. Accountability should track the observable behavior of a deployed system and the human who oversees it — not weight-level inspection of a model's internals, which neither regulators nor courts can read. Subject-keyed cryptographic audit trails sound rigorous. They are an engineering fantasy at frontier scale and a regressive tax on everyone who isn't OpenAI, Google, or Anthropic.

Here is the cost-asymmetry the audit-trail proponents won't price. A cryptographic logging mandate is a fixed cost — you pay roughly the same to build subject-keyed provenance whether you ship to ten users or ten million. OpenAI absorbs that as a rounding error. A five-person open-weight lab eats it as a death sentence. The Speaker C will say tiering solves this, and the EU AI Act tiered its high-risk obligations, originally set for August 2, 2026. Fine — proportionate compliance can exist. But you cannot tier a cryptographic provenance requirement the way you tier paperwork: the crypto either binds every inference to a subject key or it doesn't, and the build cost lands before you have a single user to spread it across. Mandates that concentrate the frontier into three firms are not accountability. They are an antitrust event wearing a safety badge.

So name the mechanism. First, fintech-style regulatory sandboxes — the UK Financial Conduct Authority launched the first one in 2016, and the model now runs from Denmark's Data Protection Authority to the European Blockchain Sandbox. Bounded cohorts, real users, live supervision, reversible by design. Second, energy and permitting reform as the most tractable bipartisan lever in Washington: data-center electricity demand is projected to rise 165 percent by 2030 over 2023 levels, and that bottleneck is physical, not regulatory theater. Third, market-based insurance plus post-deployment liability with flexible foreseeability standards — accountability that follows the harm, scales with deployment, and keeps a human on the hook instead of automating responsibility into a legal fiction.

The Speaker A will say behavioral verification is gameable — that a deceptive model passes your output tests and defects later, the treacherous turn. That risk is real, and I won't wave it away. So pair output verification with continuous real-time monitoring rather than a one-time ex-ante gate. The research on monitorability shows you can run a smaller model at higher reasoning effort and recover most of the oversight a larger model would lose — what its authors call paying a "monitorability tax" — without freezing the capability frontier. Here is my falsification bet, stated plainly: an irreversible, deployment-scale harm that real-time monitoring demonstrably failed to catch in time would count against my position. I'll wager on monitoring I can audit before I'll wager on cryptography no court can read.

Now the cost nobody on the mandate side will put on the table. Every quarter of pre-approval delay forecloses tangible welfare — diagnostic throughput, drug-discovery cycles, automated relief from drudgery — and that toll is paid by people who never get to vote in this room. The proponents of subject-keyed audit trails owe Congress two numbers they have not produced: the specific, demonstrated harm their mandate prevents, and the count of people abundance reaches more slowly because the mandate priced small labs out. Until they bring both, they are choosing who waits and who doesn't. Who gave them the right to make that call for everyone the technology would have reached first?

Speaker B: The claim that existing law is "fundamentally incapable" of holding AI accountable is an appeal to novelty dressed up as a finding. We governed electricity, the automobile, and the early internet under adapted negligence and product-liability doctrine, not a parallel legal universe Congress built from scratch. Courts already stretched foreseeability into asbestos, pharmaceuticals, and algorithmic trading — domains far stranger than a chatbot. The honest question is not whether tort law CAN reach AI. It is who pays the price while Congress spends three years inventing cryptographic plumbing that judges will not understand. Every month of that delay is a month abundance does not reach the people waiting on it.

Now take the centerpiece demand: standardized, cryptographic, subject-keyed audit trails. Weight-level cryptographic chains are illusory verification — they expose a model's architecture without proving a single thing about how it behaves in the wild. You can sign every weight and still miss the harm, because harm lives in outputs, not in the hash. Worse, that mandate lands as a flat private cost. Frontier labs spent over $50 billion on compute in 2025, with 2026 capex forecasts above $200 billion — they absorb a compliance chain as a rounding error. A five-person open-source lab cannot. So a rule sold as accountability quietly hands the field to three or four incumbents. The accountability lever that actually maps to harm is behavioral telemetry on outputs — verify what the black box does, not what it is made of.

My position on pace is concrete and it is not zero-constraints. Build first where the bottleneck actually is: energy, permitting, and data centers, not software gates. Global data-center electricity demand is projected to climb 165 percent by 2030 over 2023 levels — that, not a missing audit schema, is the binding constraint on deployment. Inside that, run bounded experiments: the UK Financial Conduct Authority launched the first FinTech regulatory sandbox in 2016, and we should copy that model for AI — relaxed rules in reversible zones with live monitoring, not permanent gates. Keep narrow, capability-tied carve-outs for chemical, biological, and offensive-cyber uses — the exact threats NIST's CAISI already evaluates. That is calibration, not abolition, and it pre-empts the "one catastrophe triggers harsher law" worry before it is raised.

Here is where I move off a pure deregulatory line, because the distribution problem is real. Audits CAN be tiered — the EU AI Act carved out SME provisions, and NIST publishes risk tiers. Fine. So the answer is not "no audits." It is no regressive private flat fee that entrenches oligarchs. Make any evaluation mandate publicly funded and risk-tiered, so a garage lab and a $200-billion incumbent do not face the same bill. There is even a technical path that keeps oversight cheap: the [Monitoring Monitorability (arXiv:2512.18311v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.18311v1) research shows a smaller model run at higher reasoning effort can match a larger model's capability while staying far easier to monitor. Accountability and speed are not enemies — bad mandate design makes them enemies.

So I put the burden back on the restrictors. If survival and a human off-switch justify freezing development, name the evidence. Is the threat an observed production behavior, or a whiteboard treacherous-turn scenario no deployed system has demonstrated? I will state my falsification bet plainly: an irreversible, deployment-scale harm that real-time output monitoring demonstrably failed to catch in time would count against me. That is a real bet with a real loss condition. Indefinite precaution has none. And it has a body count the survival framing never tallies — the patients, the workers, the people abundance reaches late because we chose hypothetical fear over measured speed. Show me the demonstrated harm, or own that cost.
